## The National — Never Tear Us Apart

**Played**: 2026-02-05

This is The National's cover of the INXS song.

- **Moment in History**: In 2015, INXS guitarist Tim Farriss said he may never play the guitar properly again after severing his finger in a boating accident in Sydney. He underwent surgery twice trying to reattach the finger but was left with permanent hand damage. 'Never Tear Us Apart,' which he played on, was named 'The Best Australian Song of All Time' on Triple J's Hottest 100 the previous year.


## The National — Murder Me Rachael

**Played**: 2026-06-11 (Segment 4 — Indie anthems)

An early National track from Sad Songs for Dirty Lovers (2003), later captured live on the Cherry Tree EP (2004). Matt Berninger wrote it about his older sister, Rachel; it's one of the earliest glimpses of the band's trademark — savage, twisted lyricism and Bryce Dessner's razor guitar — years before Alligator made them. The catalogue date here is a reissue; the song itself predates their breakthrough.


## The National — The Geese of Beverly Road

**Played**: 2026-07-30

"The Geese of Beverly Road" is the seventh track on The National's breakthrough third album Alligator, released 12 April 2005 via Beggars Banquet. The band performed the track at the wedding of producer Peter Katis — a photo of the band playing while couples danced in the foreground became the cover art for their follow-up album Boxer (2007). The song's title references an actual street. Alligator was produced by Peter Katis and Paul Mahajan at Tarquin Studios, Drummerman Studios, and other locations, received a Metacritic score of 82/100, and was the album that transformed The National from a cult concern into a critically adored force.

- **Sources**: Wikipedia · Pitchfork · The Guardian


## The National — Fake Empire

**Played**: 2026-08-13

The National are a US band (Brooklyn, New York) formed 1999 in Cincinnati, Ohio. "Fake Empire" (3:27) is track 1 on Boxer, released 22 May 2007 on Beggars Banquet Records, produced by Peter Katis and The National at Tarquin Studios in Bridgeport, Connecticut; written by Matt Berninger and Bryce Dessner. The song was released as a single 23 June 2008, the album's third and final single. Dessner built the track around a four-over-three polyrhythm in the piano; the horn fanfare was written by Padma Newsome. The National's network TV debut of the song came on The Late Show with David Letterman, 24 July 2007. An instrumental version featured in Barack Obama's 2008 presidential campaign video "Signs of Hope and Change" and the song was played at the 2008 Democratic National Convention. It also appeared in the Chuck episode "Chuck Versus the Break-up" (13 October 2008) and over the closing credits of the 2008 film Battle in Seattle.

- **Sources**: Wikipedia · Bandcamp

## Radiohead — Killer Cars (Mogadon version)

**Played**: 2026-07-15 (Segment 3) *(TikTok)*

Radiohead (formed 1985, Abingdon, Oxfordshire) released "Killer Cars (Mogadon Version)" (3:50) as a B-side on the "Just" single (21 August 1995, XL Recordings/Parlophone) — "Just" reached No. 19 on the UK Singles Chart. A separate, non-Mogadon version of the song appears on the "High & Dry / Planet Telex" single. The drum loop from "Killer Cars" became the foundation for "Planet Telex" on The Bends, which was written and recorded in a single evening at RAK Studios.

- **TikTok angle**: Deep-dive/trivia angle: the track is named after Mogadon, a brand name for the sedative nitrazepam, which fits its down-beat, meditative sound — pitched as a 1995 deep cut most listeners haven't heard.

- **Sources**: Discogs · Wikipedia · Official Charts Company

## Bob Dylan — Maggie's Farm

**Played**: 2026-03-06

Album: Bringing It All Back Home | Released: 1965 | Label: Columbia Records. A protest song that marked Dylan's shift from acoustic folk to electric rock. He famously performed it electric at the 1965 Newport Folk Festival, an event that became one of the most controversial moments in music history when folk purists booed. The song is widely interpreted as a rejection of conformity and exploitation. It has been covered by many artists, including Rage Against the Machine. The title has been adopted as political shorthand in British politics.


## Bob Dylan — Sara (Album Version)

**Played**: 2026-09-10 *(TikTok)*

"Sara" (5:31) closes Desire (track 10), co-written largely with Jacques Levy and produced by Don DeVito, released 5 January 1976 on Columbia Records. It was recorded on 31 July 1975, the final day of the Desire sessions. It is Dylan's direct address to his then-wife Sara Dylan, amid their divorce. Sara Dylan showed up at the studio and listened while Dylan recorded the song, per Jacques Levy's account in Howard Sounes's Dylan biography. Like "Visions of Johanna" a decade earlier, it is named for Sara — American Songwriter notes it would be the last song he would write for her in this direct register.

- **TikTok angle**: Dylan almost never explains his songs, but Sara is the rare one he's admitted is about his then-wife — written as a plea during their divorce, and he recorded the vocal in one take while she watched. The most private song in the Dylan catalogue. Closer energy.

- **Sources**: Wikipedia · Songfacts · American Songwriter

## Bon Iver — Blood Bank

**Played**: 2026-08-13

Bon Iver is the project of Justin Vernon, from Eau Claire, Wisconsin. "Blood Bank" (4:44) is track 1 of 4 on the Blood Bank EP, released 20 January 2009 on Jagjaguwar (US; 4AD handled some European releases). The EP's four tracks are "Blood Bank," "Beach Baby," "Babys," and "Woods." A 10th-anniversary reissue with the original tracks plus new live versions was released 27 March 2020 via Jagjaguwar; the live version of "Blood Bank" was recorded at Ericsson Globe [Rolling Stone, 21 January 2020].

## 06. Death Cab for Cutie — Punching the Flowers

Death Cab for Cutie formed in Bellingham, Washington in 1997. Ben Gibbard has led the band throughout their catalogue — *Transatlanticism* (2003), *Plans* (2005), *Narrow Stairs* (2008). "Punching the Flowers" is from *I Built You a Tower*, due June 5, 2026 on ANTI- Records, their new label. This follows 2022's *Asphalt Meadows*. At 148 BPM and 3:11, it's one of the faster Death Cab tracks — playing it tonight is a genuine pre-release first play.

**Placement**: Follows Ecca Vandal while keeping the energy high. The album doesn't officially exist yet. Worth a one-liner in the link to mark it.

## Death Cab For Cutie — Riptides

**Played**: 2026-03-19

Track 9 and lead single from Death Cab For Cutie's 11th studio album I Built You a Tower, released 16 March 2026 on ANTI-; album due 5 June 2026 — their first release on an independent label after more than 20 years on Atlantic. Produced by John Congleton and recorded in three weeks at Animal Rites in Los Angeles as well as the band members' homes in Seattle, Portland, Bellingham, and LA. The album grew from the band's 20th anniversary tours for Transatlanticism and Plans (2023-2025), during which frontman Ben Gibbard was privately dealing with the collapse of his marriage. Gibbard: 'Riptides is about the challenge of dealing with personal struggles as the world around us experiences tragedy and loss on an unfathomable scale.' The band also announced a UK/European tour including Manchester, Edinburgh, and Bristol.

## Death Cab For Cutie — Transatlanticism (demo)

**Played**: 2026-07-15 (Segment 10 — Close) *(Closer)*

Death Cab for Cutie (formed 1997, Bellingham, WA; 2003 lineup: Ben Gibbard, Chris Walla, Nick Harmer, Jason McGerr, who joined for this album) closed their fourth album Transatlanticism (7 October 2003, Barsuk Records) with a demo version of the title track (6:13). Songs from the album appeared in The O.C. and Six Feet Under, contributing to the band's mainstream breakthrough and leading to their major-label signing with Atlantic for Plans (2005).

## 14. David Bowie — Song for Bob Dylan

"Song for Bob Dylan" is track 9 on *Hunky Dory* (1971), Bowie's fourth studio album. It's a direct address to Dylan — both tribute and lamentation, referencing "the voice that left us all behind." Bowie was openly influenced by Dylan and this song documents that debt plainly. Trevor Bolder, the bassist in Bowie's Spiders from Mars band, died on **May 21, 2013** — 13 years ago today — from cancer, aged 62. Bolder played on Hunky Dory, Ziggy Stardust, Aladdin Sane, and Pin Ups before leaving the Bowie fold.

**Placement**: Closes the Moment in History segment. The Trevor Bolder connection gives it a date tie-in for the post-show TikTok. It also quietly begins the show's Bob Dylan thread — Bowie wrote about Dylan in 1971; the show will close with Nada Surf's "Blonde on Blonde," named after Dylan's 1966 double album. That connection is not announced on air.

## David Bowie — Moonage Daydream

**Played**: 2026-05-07 (Segment 4) *(TikTok)* *(moment in history)*

From The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars (June 16, 1972, RCA), one of the album's most feverish, defining tracks. Its real history begins on this date in 1971 — 55 years before this episode. Bowie released "Moonage Daydream" under the name Arnold Corns, a band he'd built around designer Freddie Burretti as the supposed frontman. It sold nothing; nobody knew it was him. He took the song back, rerecorded it, and placed it third on Ziggy Stardust. The date connection is told live on air, and the post-show TikTok carries the same story to anyone who missed the broadcast. Placement: opens the Moment in History segment — the "you've been listening to a rescued song for fifty years" angle is the show's strongest post-show revelation.

- **Moment in History**: On this date (May 7) in 1971 — 55 years before this episode aired — Bowie released "Moonage Daydream" under the fake band name Arnold Corns (fronted publicly by designer Freddie Burretti). It sold nothing and nobody knew it was Bowie; he later took the song back, rerecorded it, and placed it third on The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars (1972).

- **TikTok angle**: In 1971, on this exact date, Bowie released this song under a fake name/band (Arnold Corns) that he'd invented; it flopped and nobody knew it was him. He took it back and a year later put it on Ziggy Stardust — "you've been listening to a rescued song for fifty-five years." Framed as one of three date connections built into the show that night. Placebo released their cover of Kate Bush's "Running Up That Hill (A Deal with God)" in 2003. Placebo's version originally appeared as a B-side and on their B-sides/rarities collection Covers. ## Elliott Smith — Say Yes

**Played**: 2026-03-12

Closing track from Smith's third album Either/Or, released 25 February 1997 on Kill Rock Stars. Opening track of Led Zeppelin IV, released 8 November 1971 on Atlantic Records; also released as a single. ## Led Zeppelin — No Quarter (Remaster)

**Played**: 2026-09-03 *(Moment in History)*

Closes the A-side of Led Zeppelin's 1973 classic Houses of the Holy, written by John Paul Jones, Jimmy Page and Robert Plant — Jones in particular is often credited with its brooding, murky keyboard atmosphere. Jimmy Page applied vari-speed tape trickery to drop the whole song by a semitone, giving it a thicker, more oppressive mood than the version first sketched at Headley Grange. It became a centerpiece of every Zeppelin concert through the band's final tour; this "Remaster" is the 2014 reissue treatment from the deluxe edition.

- **Moment in History**: In 2023, an album sleeve signed by all four members of Led Zeppelin sold for £15,000 at auction despite not containing the actual record — the cardboard sleeve of Houses of the Holy (this album) had only been estimated to sell for £1,200–£1,800. Items signed by all band members are rare due to drummer John Bonham's 1980 death and the band's subsequent split; the seller acquired the autographs during a chance encounter at Gatwick Airport in 1977.

## 13. Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young — Ohio

"Ohio" was written by Neil Young within days of the Kent State massacre on May 4, 1970, in which National Guard soldiers fired on unarmed student protesters opposing the US invasion of Cambodia, killing four and wounding nine. CSNY recorded and released the track within weeks — one of the fastest protest songs ever committed to record and distributed. "Tin soldiers and Nixon coming / we're finally on our own." It reached #14 on the Billboard Hot 100 in June 1970. The track appears here from the *So Far* compilation (1974).

**Placement**: Follows Marvin Gaye in the history segment as its natural companion — both tracks are direct political responses to American violence in the same period, both recorded at speed out of urgency. The two tracks together make an argument without a word from the desk.

**Played**: 2026-06-04 (Segment 4 — Moment in History) *(moment in history)*

Frankie Goes to Hollywood were a Liverpool synth-pop band formed in 1980, fronted by Holly Johnson, two studio albums before disbanding in 1987. "Two Tribes," produced by Trevor Horn, entered the UK Singles Chart at number one on June 10, 1984 and stayed there for nine consecutive weeks — the longest-running number-one single of the 1980s in the UK. During those nine weeks, their previous single "Relax" climbed back to number two, giving the band the top two positions simultaneously. The track won the 1984 Ivor Novello Award for Best Song Musically and Lyrically. The music video depicted Ronald Reagan and Konstantin Chernenko fighting, a direct satire of the Cold War nuclear arms race. Second in the Moment in History segment, immediately following The Jam — the anti-war thread intensifies from punk defiance to full nuclear satire.

- **Moment in History**: "Two Tribes" was released on this date, 4th June 1984, via ZTT Records.

## 10. Ramones — Blitzkrieg Bop *(moment in history)*

From the Ramones' self-titled debut album, released on Sire Records on **23rd April 1976** — fifty years ago today.

The cover photograph was taken by punk photographer Roberta Bayley, depicting the band against a brick wall. It cost the record company £92.

The album was 29 minutes long. It sold almost nothing on release. What it did was establish the template for punk rock — short songs, fast tempos, distorted guitars, and a complete absence of interest in the prevailing musical culture. Every punk band that followed owes something to it.

Opens the Moment in History segment. The 50th anniversary is the peg.

Opening track on the self-titled album, released March 1967 (as a single in December 1966) on Verve Records. The last song recorded for the album, added at the request of producer Tom Wilson who wanted a potential single. ## Art of Noise feat. Tom Jones — Kiss

**Played**: 2026-05-07 (Segment 4) *(moment in history)*

Art of Noise were an avant-garde synth-pop group whose membership included Anne Dudley — born on this date in 1956, turning 70 on the day of this episode. Dudley is also a composer, conductor, and keyboardist who won the Oscar for Best Original Musical or Comedy Score for The Full Monty in 1998. "Kiss" — a radical reimagining of the Prince original, pairing Tom Jones's voice with the group's mechanical precision — reached UK No.5 in 1988. Taken here from The Best of the Art of Noise (1992). Placement: closes the Moment in History segment — three tracks, three date connections, three very different decades; the Anne Dudley / Full Monty / Tom Jones triangle is a compelling post-show reveal.

- **Moment in History**: Art of Noise member Anne Dudley was born on this date (May 7) in 1956 — turning 70 on the day this episode aired. She later won the Oscar for Best Original Musical or Comedy Score for The Full Monty (1998). Art of Noise's "Kiss" with Tom Jones reached UK No.5 in 1988.

---

## Art of Noise

- **Origin**: London, England · formed 1983 · disbanded/reformed intermittently, sporadically active since
- **Members**: Anne Dudley (keyboards, arrangement), Trevor Horn (production), J.J. Jeczalik (programming), Gary Langan (engineering), Paul Morley (concept/lyrics); Horn and Morley departed after an acrimonious split from ZTT in 1985. Featured vocalist on "Kiss": Tom Jones, Welsh singer known for "It's Not Unusual" and "Delilah."

- **Facts**:

## Carl Sagan — A Glorious Dawn

**Played**: 2026-07-30 *(Moment in History)* *(TikTok)*

"A Glorious Dawn" is the first track from John Boswell's Symphony of Science project, which uses Auto-Tune to set Carl Sagan's spoken words from Cosmos to music. Boswell — a musician and science communicator working under the name melodysheep — created the track in 2009, sampling Sagan's "Across the sea of space" and "A still more glorious dawn" passages alongside Stephen Hawking's "We are just an advanced breed of monkeys." The video went viral upon release. Jack White's Third Man Records pressed it as a special 7-inch vinyl single for the 75th anniversary of Carl Sagan's birth, on 9 November 2009. The Symphony of Science project has since grown to dozens of songs sampling various scientists.

- **Moment in History**: On this date, 30 July 2016, Third Man Records celebrated its seventh anniversary by launching a specially engineered turntable, The Icarus Craft, into space via high-altitude balloon — playing the very first vinyl record in space. The 45 RPM single played was "A Glorious Dawn." The craft reached over 94,000 feet during its 80-minute flight before the balloon burst and it dropped back to Earth.

- **TikTok angle**: Pitched as scratching "an itch only auto-tuned Carl Sagan could scratch," tied to the fact this collaboration was the record launched into space for Third Man Records' 7th anniversary.

- **Sources**: Wikipedia · SymphonyofScience.com · LA Beat

## Lynyrd Skynyrd — Free Bird

**Played**: 2026-07-30

"Free Bird" was recorded on 3 April 1973 at Studio One in Doraville, Georgia and released on Lynyrd Skynyrd's debut album in August 1973. The opening line — "If I leave here tomorrow, would you still remember me?" — was a question guitarist Allen Collins' girlfriend Kathy asked him. The song's famous nine-minute runtime (album version 9:08) was nearly cut by the record company who thought it was too long for radio. The extended guitar solos were originally added to give singer Ronnie Van Zant a break during the band's multi-set club shows. The piano intro was written by roadie Billy Powell, who upon hearing they'd included it, formally joined as the band's keyboardist. The song reached #19 on the Billboard Hot 100 in January 1975, was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2008, and has become one of the most requested songs in FM radio history. The tradition of shouting "Free Bird!" at concerts — regardless of the performer — originated from Skynyrd's live shows.

## The Bobby Fuller Four — I Fought the Law (Single Version)

**Played**: 2026-08-20 *(moment in history)*

Written in 1958 by Sonny Curtis, who became the Crickets' guitarist by replacing Buddy Holly — the Fuller Four's 1966 Mustang/Del-Fi re-recording (produced by Bob Keane, the man behind Ritchie Valens) turned it into a top-10 US hit (#9) [unverified — Wikipedia only]. Fuller first cut it in 1964 on his own Exeter label in El Paso, where it was only a regional West Texas hit — so the famous 'single version' is actually a rerecord [unverified — Wikipedia only]. Fuller died mysteriously at 23 in July 1966, weeks after the song finally broke nationally; his death in his parked car — ruled accidental, but long suspected to be foul play — remains one of rock's unsolved cases. Ranked #175 on Rolling Stone's 2004 list of the 500 Greatest Songs and named to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame's '500 Songs That Shaped Rock' — The Clash's 1979 cover made it a punk-age anthem [unverified — Wikipedia only].

## The B-52's — Rock Lobster

**Played**: 2026-03-19

First recorded and released on DB Records in April 1978 (the label's very first release), then re-recorded for the band's self-titled debut album on Warner Bros., July 1979. Written by Fred Schneider and Ricky Wilson. Recorded on a shoestring budget of around $700 at Mountain Studios in Atlanta; a key on Kate Pierson's Farfisa organ didn't work. The iconic bass line was played by Pierson on a Korg SB-100 synth, not a bass guitar. Pierson and Cindy Wilson's fish noises are a tribute to Yoko Ono. John Lennon heard the song playing in a Bermuda disco in 1979 and it inspired him to break his five-year recording hiatus. Rolling Stone ranked it number 147 on their 500 Greatest Songs list. The band name comes from the beehive hairstyles worn by Kate Pierson and Cindy Wilson, resembling the nose cone of a B-52 bomber.
